nameStory: The 'flamed' tigersnail gets its fiery name from the beautiful reddish-brown streaks and bands that sweep across its shell like flames dancing around its coils. The 'tiger' part refers to these bold, striped patterns that reminded early naturalists of a tiger's markings, while 'disc' describes its relatively flat, coin-like shape when viewed from above.
description: The Flamed Tigersnail is a small land snail with a distinctively flattened, disc-shaped shell that's beautifully decorated with flame-like reddish-brown bands. This is actually the most common and widespread tigersnail in North America, making it a great species for beginning snail enthusiasts to learn. The shell typically measures about half an inch across and has a smooth, somewhat glossy surface. Like all land snails, it carries its home on its back and extends soft tentacles with eyes at the tips when it's actively moving around.

idTips.label: Flame-like shell patterns
idTips.description: Look for distinctive reddish-brown streaks and bands that spiral around the shell like flames - these markings are irregular and wavy, not straight lines

idTips.label: Flattened disc shape
idTips.description: The shell is notably flat and wide rather than tall and pointed, resembling a small coin or button when viewed from above

idTips.label: Smooth shell texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth and somewhat glossy to the touch, without obvious ridges or bumps, though you may feel very fine growth lines

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: About the size of a dime or smaller, typically around half an inch across, with the width much greater than the height

idTips.label: Shell opening shape
idTips.description: The opening (aperture) is crescent-shaped and relatively wide, taking up a good portion of the shell's underside

habitat: Flamed Tigersnails prefer moist, shaded areas in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, often hiding under logs, leaf litter, or rocks during dry periods. They're particularly fond of rich, organic soil with plenty of decaying plant matter, and you'll often find them in areas with maple, oak, and beech trees. Look for them in ravines, along stream banks, or in any woodland area that stays consistently damp.

seasonality.spring: Active after snow melts, emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and deep leaf litter. This is an excellent time to spot them as they move around more in the cool, moist conditions.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods and after rain showers, but they retreat into hiding during hot, dry spells. Early morning or evening searches are most productive.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily before winter, making this one of the best times for observation. They're preparing for hibernation and can often be found moving across trails.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden deep under logs, rocks, or buried in leaf litter where they won't freeze. Rarely visible unless you're doing serious digging in their habitat.

funFact: Despite being called a 'tigersnail,' these little creatures are actually more like tiny ecosystem recyclers - they have a special stomach compartment filled with microscopic stones and grit that they use like a rock tumbler to grind up tough plant material and fungi, helping break down forest debris into rich soil.
confusionNotes: The flame patterns are the key distinguishing feature from other small woodland snails - most similar species either lack these distinctive reddish streaks entirely or have much more regular, straight-lined patterns. Memory trick: 'Flames flicker and dance' - the irregular, wavy flame patterns never form perfectly straight lines.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the intimidating scientific name fool you - 'Anguispira' comes from Latin words meaning 'snake coil,' referring to how the shell spirals, not because it has anything to do with actual snakes. The 'alternata' part refers to the alternating light and dark pattern of the flame markings.
compareHints: Since this is the only tigersnail species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small woodland snails in the disc snail family. Other disc snails typically lack the distinctive flame-like reddish markings and tend to be more uniformly colored in browns or grays. The Flamed Tigersnail's bold patterning makes it one of the more distinctively marked small snails you'll encounter in New England forests.
